passage: Two weeks before Sangeeta's board exams the power cuts started, and the sisters studied by the light of a rechargeable lamp. Gargi's instinct was to keep guiding; time was short. Instead she slid her chair back. 'Do the next three without me. I'll check at the end.' Sangeeta looked up, alarmed. 'What if I get stuck?' Diwali night.
Dear diary, so many relatives came today! Everyone asked the same question: 'Vikas, what will you become?' And I said ENGINEER every time, loud, like Papa taught me. Papa is an engineer, Dada was an engineer, and Mridul Bhaiya is doing engineering in Pune. Bua pinched my cheek and said, 'Our family's fourth engineer!' Everyone clapped. I felt so proud, like I had already passed. Then on the terrace, while we lit phuljhadis, Mridul Bhaiya asked me quietly, 'What do you actually like doing?' I said engineering. He said, 'No, like, what makes you forget time?' I said drawing comics. He laughed and said engineers can draw too. I don't know why that question made my tummy feel funny. Anyway, I'm going to be an engineer.
Vikas

passage: During the rice-sowing rains, when the village school closed early, Aparna stood on the mud wall and announced to the goats and to Kamal, 'I am going to be a doctor. Monday, 10 pm.
Stream forms went in today. I ticked Science (PCM) without even reading the other options. Papa and I decided this years ago, or Papa decided and I agreed, which is the same thing, I think. Everyone in our family is in science. When Ma'am asked if I was sure, I said, 'Totally,' and I meant it. So why did I feel nothing? Not happy, not sad. Just flat, like soda left open overnight. Nandini ticked Humanities and practically danced out of the room. She's going to do psychology and has already read three books about it. I've never read a physics book that wasn't for an exam. Whatever. It's decided. That's a relief, actually. No more thinking about it.
Baljeet, go to bed.

qa.a: Baljeet could read a physics book not meant for exams, or talk honestly with Papa and a school counsellor about what sparks interest.

qa.a: Nandini is excited and eager, because she chose Humanities after actually reading about psychology.

'Army,' he said when the headmaster asked. 'Army,' when the shopkeeper asked. Madhav, his cousin, was different, always taking apart old radios, arguing with himself about electronics or music. One evening on the terrace, Madhav asked, 'If nobody in the family had joined, would you still?' Naveen opened his mouth to say yes. Nothing came. He shrugged. 'It's decided.' passage: By October Arohi had been three different people. In June she hung out with the debate kids and wore her hair in a tight bun. In August she dyed a blue streak into it, joined the skateboarding group at the promenade and stopped answering debate texts. Now she mostly ate lunch alone in the library, headphones in, listening to old Hindi songs she would never admit to liking. At dinner in the Andheri flat, her brother Darshan joked, 'Which Arohi are we getting today?' She slammed down her spoon. 'Why does everyone want me to be ONE thing?' and walked out. Later, in her room, she scrolled through photos of all three versions and couldn't tell which one was real. Darshan knocked and slid a plate of mango slices under the door.

qa.a: A blue streak.

qa.a: Arohi felt confused and unsettled, unable to tell which version of herself was real.

qa.a: He could stop joking about her changes and simply spend time with her, letting her know it's normal to try different selves.

qa.a: Darshan probably feels sorry the joke hurt, which is why he quietly slides mango slices under the door.

passage: In the kasba of Chandpur, people had opinions about Himani. She had done a year of agriculture at the district college, then switched to a BA, then spent the summer volunteering at the anganwadi and the monsoon travelling with a folk theatre troupe to twelve villages. Asif, who ran the mobile repair shop and had known her since school, teased her across the counter. 'Next month, astronaut?' Himani laughed, but she showed him her notebook. On each page: what she had tried, what she felt doing it, what it said about what she valued. 'The anganwadi and the theatre have the same thing,' she said. passage: Beatriz had left her law degree in Porto after one year, and for eleven months she had been 'figuring things out'. She worked mornings at a surf shop, tried a pottery class twice, started three language courses online and finished none. Every Sunday she told her mother she was exploring. This Sunday she met Clara, her old school friend, for coffee. Clara had also switched courses, from biology to nursing, but only after shadowing at a clinic for a month and keeping a journal. 'How did you know?' Beatriz asked. Clara shrugged. 'I didn't at first. I tested it.' Walking home along the river, Beatriz realised she hadn't tested anything; she had just floated. That night she wrote two questions on a napkin: What did I actually enjoy? What would I do for free?
